How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour-nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour-nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival
                    1
                    . Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells
                    2,3
                    . The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported
                    4,5
                    . Here we used
                    iFlpMosaics
                    and
                    iSuRe
                    –HadCre
                    to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These
                    Vegfr2
                    -knockout (
                    Vegfr2
                    
                      KO
                    
                    ) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs.
                    Vegfr2
                    
                      KO
                    
                    ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF,
                    Vegfr2
                    
                      KO
                    
                    ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of
                    Vegfr2
                    
                      KO
                    
                    ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age
                    1–3
                    . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested
                    4
                    , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 
                    bp
                    (calibrated years before present or 1950 
                    ce
                    ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 
                    bp
                    ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 
                    bp
                    ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts
                    5–8
                    . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory
                    9
                    and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
abstract: Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient -1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy.

title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
abstract: Sub-ångström spatial resolution combined with attosecond temporal resolution enables direct observation of electron motion in matter1. Attosecond hard X-ray pulses generated at X-ray free-electron laser sources provide the requisite spatiotemporal sensitivity, yet their application has been limited by the absence of precise pulse metrology and control. Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Field-correlation measurements provide the first time-domain characterization of the pulse coherence time and demonstrate attosecond synchronization between the generated pulse pairs. By exploiting non-sequential two-photon absorption as a nonlinear probe, intensity autocorrelation quantifies the average pulse duration directly in the time domain to be 170 as. The demonstrated experimental tools and techniques enable systematic attosecond time-resolved experiments, including X-ray pump-X-ray probe spectroscopy and diffraction, and open a pathway to probing electronic phenomena with unprecedented spatial-temporal resolution.

title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
abstract: Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π-π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates.

title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Mycobacterium
                    tuberculosis
                    , the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen
                    1
                    . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations
                    2,3
                    . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium
                    Mycobacterium smegmatis
                    and the pathogen
                    M. tuberculosis
                    . These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions
                    4
                    for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment
                    1–8
                    , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear
                    9–13
                    . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies
                    1
                    , but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale
                    2–6
                    . This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction
                    4–6
                    . Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.

title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
abstract: The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1-3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies.

title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD
                    1–3
                    . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge
                    4
                    . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals
                    5
                    , and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts
                    6,7
                    ; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown
                    8,9
                    . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene
                    CHD8
                    and candidates including
                    REST
                    . Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals
                    10
                    , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher
                    ZFX
                    expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

title: Photocatalytic therapy via cross-coupling hydrogen evolution in cancer cells
abstract: Zhou et al. develop an oxygen-independent photocatalytic strategy that converts glutathione to its oxidized form while generating hydrogen in cancer cells, thereby disrupting the intracellular redox balance. This catalytic redox remodeling induces ferroptosis and antitumor immune activation, establishing an oxygen-independent mode of photocatalytic cancer therapy.

title: π‐Extended Bisallyls Through Valence Isomerism: From Transient Diradicals to Persistent Anions
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Bisallyl diradicals are central intermediates in allene dimerization, yet they are normally too short‐lived to observe under thermal conditions. Here, π‐extension of Staudinger‐type allene dimers weakens the central cyclobutane bond sufficiently to make reversible ring opening accessible near room temperature. Variable‐temperature NMR spectroscopy and ROESY exchange correlations reveal repeated cleavage and reformation of this bond, with activation free energies of 15.77 and 13.79 kcal mol −1 for the Staudinger dimer and its π‐expanded analogue, respectively. Calculations reproduce this trend and identify low‐population open‐shell singlet bisallyls as the intermediates, while explaining the absence of neutral‐state EPR signals. Reduction reverses the relative stability of the closed and open valence isomers. Voltammetry and chemical reduction support a sequence of ring‐opened radical‐anion, dianion, and tetraanion states. The dianion is characterized by NMR spectroscopy and x‐ray diffraction, while spectroscopy and calculations reveal progressive bond redistribution from mixed‐valence allyl‐radical/allyl‐anion character to two allyl‐anion units and, finally, four fluorenyl‐anion‐like termini. These results connect hidden neutral diradicals with persistent reduced bisallyl frameworks through charge‐controlled covalent‐bond reorganization.

title: Fluorinated Fullerene Derivatives for Thermally Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT PCBM (phenyl‐C 61 ‐butyric acid methyl ester) is one of the most used electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, PCBM tends to self‐aggregate during the thermal aging process, disrupting film continuity and limiting device lifetime. To address this issue, we synthesized new fluorinated phenyl fullerene derivatives, FPCPB and 5FPCPB, forming a composite fullerene ETL by blending with PCBM. We found that fullerene self‐aggregation was suppressed through the synergistic effects of weak interactions, such as π–π conjugation between phenyl and fluorophenyl groups and C─H···F van der Waals interactions, and the constrained molecular conformation induced by intermolecular steric hindrance, thereby markedly improving film uniformity and thermal stability, reducing defect‐state density, and suppressing ion migration. In addition, the energy level alignment between perovskite and ETL is optimized, enhancing electron transport. Ultimately, 5FPCPB, having more compatible energy levels and stronger conjugation effects than FPCPB, achieved a 26.42% power conversion efficiency (PCE), with improved operational and thermal stability (T 90 under light = 1200 h; T 95 under 85°C > 700 h). The fullerene co‐doping strategy opens a new pathway for achieving high‐performance and thermally stable perovskite devices.

title: Dimerization‐Enabled Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence and 500‐Fold Enhanced Emission in Gold Nanoclusters
abstract: ABSTRACT Gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) are promising luminescent materials with broad applications in sensing, bioimaging, and photonics. However, highly emissive thiolate‐protected Au NCs remain difficult to access because conformational relaxation of ligands and flexible Au–thiolate motifs often promote nonradiative relaxation. Herein, we show that dimerization can switch on thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) in non‐fluorescent Au NCs thus realizing the boost of quantum yield. Upon introduction of diphosphine ligands, Au 18 (SR) 14 undergoes assembly into a tethered dimer, (Au 18 )–(Au 2 S 3 )–(Au 18 ). This structural reorganization spatially separates the HOMO and LUMO over two Au 18 units, resulting in a small singlet–triplet energy gap (0.061 eV) and enabling reverse intersystem crossing. As a result, the non‐emissive monomer is converted into a highly emissive dimer with a photoluminescence quantum yield boosted from ∼0.1% to 50%. This work identifies dimerization as an effective strategy to activate the emission of dark NCs and establishes a design principle for TADF‐type metal nanoclusters.

title: Control of Sequences and H‐Bonding Motifs in IEM‐Derived Copolymers Enables Mechanical Tunability, Self‐Healing, and Clusterization‐Triggered Emission
abstract: ABSTRACT The chemical identity and spatial arrangement of hydrogen‐bonding (H‐bonding) motifs along a polymer chain influence mechanical property, but their coupled effects on stiffness, self‐healing, and optical activity within a well‐defined backbone remain largely unexplored. Here, we install single, double, and quadruple H‐bonding motifs (including urethane, urea, aliphatic, and aromatic variants) into methyl methacrylate‐co‐butyl acrylate gradient copolymers (MMA‐ g ‐BA) via ATRP, using 2‐isocyanatoethyl methacrylate (IEM) as a versatile reactive pendant side‐chain handle. Systematic evaluation reveals that mechanical performance is governed by motif identity and chain architecture rather than H‐bond density alone. Young's moduli span nearly two orders of magnitude (29‐640 MPa), while the quadruple H‐bonding gradient copolymer achieves an excellent balance of stiffness (∼262 MPa) and toughness (∼20 MJ m −3 ), together with efficient self‐healing, recovering >90% of Young's modulus within 0.5 h and 80% of toughness after 3 h at 90°C. We further report, for the first time, clusterization‐triggered emission (CTE) in the aliphatic MMA‐ g ‐BA matrix, with quadruple H‐bonding motifs enhancing photoluminescence by promoting emissive cluster aggregation, evidenced by a lower critical cluster concentration than the unfunctionalized matrix. These findings establish motif selection and sequence control as coupled design parameters for simultaneously programming mechanical, self‐healing, and photoluminescent properties in a single poly(acrylate/methacrylate) platform.

title: Atroposelective Access to Bicyclic Peptides via an Amide Photocaging Strategy
abstract: ABSTRACT The fungal toxin α‐amanitin is a structurally complex bicyclic octapeptide featuring a macrolactam scaffold stabilized by a tryptathionine crossbridge critical for its conformational stability. Building on the prior development of the ansamer ( P ansa /M ansa ) nomenclature for an amatoxin isomer classification, the challenge of atroposelective synthesis of both isomers, the natural P ansa and non‐natural M ansa, remained. This work introduces an innovative amide bond photocaging strategy implemented on monocyclic peptide precursors, enabling the control of conformational selectivity during bicyclization to achieve the directed formation of the P ansa or M ansa atropisomer. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics simulations provide strong theoretical support for the experimentally observed atroposelectivity in M ansa formation. The methodology described could establish a paradigm for conformational control in the synthesis of bicyclic peptides, with implications for a rational conformational design across diverse peptide architectures.

title: Enantioconvergent and Regioselective Deaminative Alkenylation of α‐Amino Acid Derivatives With Internal Alkynes
abstract: ABSTRACT In this study, we disclose the first regio‐ and enantioselective deaminative alkenylation of amino acid derivatives with internal alkynes. This Ni‐catalyzed protocol provides direct access to chiral homoallylic carbonyl compounds from abundant amino acid building blocks and readily available alkynes. The transformation proceeds with excellent E / Z stereoselectivity and high levels of regio‐ and enantioselectivity, while accommodating a broad range of functional groups and both symmetrical and unsymmetrical internal alkynes. The synthetic utility of the method is demonstrated through the preparation and diversification of structurally complex molecules. Overall, this work establishes a general platform for enantioconvergent amino acid‐derived alkenylation and expands access to chiral homoallylic carbonyl frameworks from simple amino acid precursors.

title: Direct Evidence of Intermediate Oxygen Species Evolution in Cathode Oxides With Nominally Stable Superstructure
abstract: ABSTRACT Anionic redox has fundamentally transformed the traditional approach to developing advanced cathode materials for secondary batteries. Nevertheless, how oxygen anions participate in the redox reaction and evolve during the dynamic intercalation process remains a topic of intense controversy, particularly in prototypical materials featuring a stable superstructure. Herein, we showcase that the oxidized oxygen species at the top of charge of ribbon‐ordered P2‐Na 0.6 Li 0.2 Mn 0.8 O 2 continuously evolve during electrochemical cycling—shifting from a mixture of electron holes on O 2− and dimerized (O 2 ) n− to a mixture of (O 2 ) n− and molecular O 2 . The intermediate oxygen species increasingly stabilize as molecular O 2 instead of (O 2 ) n− , a process coupled with the expansion of Li‐vacancy clusters and the growth of Mn‐enriched domains. We further demonstrate the same trend in the P3 analogue, which features a more stable ribbon superstructure with a topological “− α − γ −” stacking pattern (“− α − β −” for P2‐Na 0.6 Li 0.2 Mn 0.8 O 2 ), further corroborating that molecular O 2 formation is inescapable even when Mn migration is restricted in the pristine structure. Collectively, our results provide direct evidence that electron holes on O 2− are unstable upon cycling and identify molecular O 2 as the ultimate oxygen‐redox product for cathode oxides with nominally stable superstructure.

title: Resurrecting Robust CYP152 Peroxygenases for Versatile Biocatalysis
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Cytochrome P450 CYP152s are attractive biocatalysts which catalyze decarboxylation and hydroxylation of fatty acids using H 2 O 2 as a co‐substrate (peroxygenase activity). Contemporary CYP152s have limited stability and substrate scope. Here we characterized eight reconstructed variants of CYP152 obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR). The results showed that variants remote from Jeotgalicoccus sp. 8456 (CYP152L1) in the tree used for the ASR tended to catalyze hydroxylation, while nodes closer to CYP152L1 favored decarboxylation; this transition correlates with Q85H substitution and FG‐loop insertion alongside other structural features. Three reconstructed variants exhibit high T m (66°C–76°C), tolerance to solvents, H 2 O 2 , extreme pH, and use non‐native substrates. CYP152‐AncG2 can catalyze one‐pot chemoenzymatic C─C bond coupling reactions to synthesize methoxy stilbene and can serve as a template for directed evolution. X‐ray structure at 1.83 Å and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicate that loop structures, surface salt bridges, and optimized access tunnels in CYP152‐AncG2 are key for enabling its superior features. These findings provide insights into the structural and evolutionary features of robust peroxygenase templates for expanding peroxygenase biocatalysis.

title: Cu‐Bi 2 O 3 /g‐C 3 N 4 Single‐Atom Catalysts for Boosting Near‐Infrared Light‐Driven Liquid Biomass Valorization
abstract: ABSTRACT A critical obstacle to achieving high overall energy conversion efficiency in mild‐condition photocatalytic biomass upgrading is insufficient exploitation of near‐infrared (NIR) light within solar spectrum. In this study, we report a photocatalyst (CBC‐X) constructed by grafting a copper single atom (Cu SA ) onto Bi 2 O 3 /g‐C 3 N 4 (BC) heterojunction, where Cu SA serves as an electron‐capture center and synergizes with the interfacial built‐in electric field (IEF) to accelerate interfacial carrier redistribution and improve charge utilization. CBC‐2 enables efficient NIR‐light‐driven esterification of liquid biomass into biofuel with a high yield of 98.9%. Additional temperature‐controlled monochromatic irradiation experiments revealed that CBC‐2 maintained a pronounced NIR‐light‐promoted catalytic response, exhibiting approximately 3.91‐ and 5.60‐fold higher average net methyl oleate formation rates than the BC heterojunction under 800 and 980 nm illumination, respectively. Infrared thermal imaging revealed a more pronounced apparent NIR‐induced heating response for CBC‐2, while temperature‐controlled catalytic experiments demonstrated the contribution of thermal conditions to the overall esterification performance. This work encourages the targeted design of a new theoretical foundation and technical pathway for designing NIR‐responsive photocatalysts of high performance, advancing the green valorization of liquid biomass.

title: Decoupling Oxygen Reduction From Hydrogen Oxidation on Platinum via Phosphorus Coordination for Reversal‐Tolerant and Durable PEM Fuel Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT During the start‐up/shut‐down (SU/SD) processes of proton‐exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), anode reversal generates an excessively high voltage that accelerates corrosion of the cathode Pt/C catalyst. Conventional approaches focus on blocking the delivery of oxygen or electrons to the anode, but fail to address the intrinsic activity coupling of Pt/C for both hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Here, we report a strategy that can selectively tailor the catalytic function of Pt nanoparticles. We used phosphorus to modulate the electronic structure of low‐loading Pt clusters on a carbon support, forming a Pt/P‐BP catalyst. The P‐coordination downshifts the d ‐band center of Pt cluster, as evidenced by in situ ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy and DFT calculations, thereby widening the activity gap between HOR and ORR. Specifically, compared to Pt/C, Pt/P‐BP enhances HOR mass activity by fivefold while substantially suppressing ORR, transforming Pt from a bifunctional catalyst into a highly selective HOR catalyst. Consequently, Pt/P‐BP achieves a 10.8‐fold higher HOR/ORR selectivity than Pt/C. In SU/SD experiments, the Pt/P‐BP anode significantly reduces carbon corrosion of the cathode catalyst layer, maintaining the fuel cell performance better than Pt/C. This work paves a new avenue toward durable PEMFCs and inspires the selectivity design for electrocatalysts.

title: The Crystal Structural Foundation of the “Rippled” Beta‐Sheet
abstract: ABSTRACT The “rippled” β‐sheet was theorized by Pauling and Corey in 1953, yet, unlike the pleated β‐sheet, remained obscure for well over half a century. From 2011 onward, the studies conducted independently by the Schneider, Nilsson and Raskatov laboratories provided the critical nucleus of biophysical data to support the viability of the rippled sheet, stimulating the ensuing x‐ray structural work. The first rippled sheet crystal structure was reported by us in 2022, 69 years after its prediction. The field has since witnessed a rapid expansion in terms of both crystal structural understanding and conceptual innovation concerning novel motif types. We have reported fifteen rippled sheet crystal structures thus far. Of the 20 canonical amino acids, our published studies have established 13 to be ripple‐genic, that is, capable of forming rippled sheets. Reported ripple‐genic systems range from tri‐ to heptapeptide in length. Among the newest advances are the mixed chirality motifs, capable of forming rippled sheets from single components, as well as conformationally locked rippled sheet macrocycles. The maturing crystal structural foundation is expected to stimulate many new and interesting applications including biomaterials, as well as molecular recognition of intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides.

title: Why sulfur stays present but inaccessible in practical lithium-sulfur pouch cells
abstract: Sulfur can remain physically present in a lithium-sulfur pouch cell while becoming electrochemically inaccessible. This perspective links local electrolyte availability and the transport of lithium ions and soluble sulfur species to sulfur conversion, lithium-metal degradation, and variations in pressure and temperature. Two qualitative diagnostic questions and a staged validation protocol guide regional failure analysis and the translation of laboratory strategies into practical cells.

title: Electrochemical Capture and Accumulation of Uranium Using a Layered Uvanite Electrode
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Extracting uranyl ions (UO22+) from uranium mining leachates can enhance national uranium security and mitigate the environmental impact of nuclear energy. Conventional techniques such as ion exchange and iron-based reductive precipitation have notable limitations. This study reports that the uvanite (U2V6O21) electrode, a layered uranium-vanadium oxide, enables potentiodynamic decoupling of UO22+ and proton intercalation/deintercalation, as well as proton-induced UO22+/UO3 precipitation and dissolution reactions. Building on a comprehensive understanding of charge-transfer and transport mechanisms, we found that potentiodynamic modulation enables selective capture of uranium species using a uvanite electrode. By allowing competing cations to deintercalate at lower potentials and preventing proton deintercalation, UO3 dissolution is inhibited, achieving a high UO3 recovery capacity of 515 mg/g at 10 times the competing cation concentration. The new electrochemistry of the uvanite electrode helps develop cost-effective, sustainable battery electrodes for critical ion extraction from water.

title: Short stories about the stability of matter
abstract: Originally, the stability of matter was a spectacular problem concerning why atoms and solids do not collapse to a point. In this Matter of Opinion, we take the liberty of combining the original non-collapse problem with the related problems of the stability of atoms and solids against dissociation and ionization. Remarkably few rigorous results are known, reflecting the complexity of quantum many-body systems, and in many situations, we must remain within the paradigm of conjectures, or even “empirical conjectures.” We follow a sequence of short stories ranging from Heisenberg, Pauli, and Oppenheimer to Dyson, Lieb, and Zhislin, showing how atoms and crystals avoid collapse and organize into stable structures. Along the way, we invoke Gauss’s theorem, discuss crystal packing through the celebrated Kepler conjecture, and conclude with a seemingly universal conjecture about crystallization that nevertheless fails.

title: Matter by design: Reflections on six decades in materials chemistry
abstract: Herein, Prof. Geoffrey A. Ozin reflects on nearly six decades in academia, as an expert at the forefront of materials chemistry and nanotechnology. From fundamental molecular structure to multi-scale hierarchies, self-assembly to synthetic fabrication, properties to functionalities, Ozin discusses lessons learned, paradigm changes, and turning points. From experimental means to emerging AI methods, Ozin projects a merger of design and discovery, stemming from a simple question that spans the entirety of materials science: can matter itself be designed?

title: The manuscript of Theseus and conceptual provenance
Atom transfer radical polymerization for sustainable processes and materials
abstract: Atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) combines increasingly sustainable polymerization processes with precise macromolecular engineering to create materials with extended lifetimes, improved circularity, and advanced functions for energy technologies. This perspective discusses recent advances and future opportunities for greener, scalable ATRP processes and the design of high-performance polymeric materials that integrate functionality and sustainability.

title: Re-directing and re-distributing Lichtenberg discharges—A new type of injection barrier on dielectrics
abstract: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg’s 1777 seminal discovery of fractal electric-discharge patterns (Lichtenberg figures) and later findings of related fulgurites are briefly recounted. Inspired by these, University of Connecticut researchers created ordered montmorillonite nano-coatings that form a barrier and redirect carriers in-plane, effectively protecting insulation materials from intense charge injection and electric discharge.

title: Cellular protein delivery through cell-penetrating peptide-mediated water pores driven by membrane potential
abstract: Combining quantitative live-cell imaging, electrophysiology, and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we establish a mechanism by which CPP additives drive the direct translocation of proteins across cellular membranes through membrane potential-dependent water pores. This framework provides a basis for intracellular delivery of protein therapeutics to expand access to intracellular, previously undruggable targets.

title: Annulation reactions by intramolecular cross-electrophile coupling
abstract: Intramolecular cross-electrophile coupling (iXEC) offers a unified strategy for building semisaturated rings directly from simple dielectrophiles. This work establishes conditions that generate persistent nickel intermediates capable of rapid radical capture through solvent-controlled activation of aryl and alkyl electrophiles. The approach enables efficient access to heteroaromatic, spirocyclic, and macrocyclic compounds under mild conditions, thus providing a broadly applicable platform for pharmaceuticals and natural products where arrays of diverse ring systems can be synthesized from a single core.

title: Relay Catalysis on Phase‐Separated Janus–CuCo Alloys for Efficient Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction at Industrial Low Concentration
abstract: ABSTRACT Earth‐abundant Cu and Co are attractive electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO 3 − RR); however, conventional solid‐solution alloys with single‐phase active sites lack effective intermediate spillover, impeding the hydrogenation of multiple reaction intermediates and limiting NH 3 selectivity under dilute nitrate conditions. Here we report phase‐separated yet electronically coupled Janus–CuCo alloys synthesized via a time–charge regulated electrochemical reduction strategy, forming metallic Cu/Co domains with a well‐defined interphase electronic structure. This Janus architecture enables relay catalysis, in which Cu domains activate NO 3 − , intermediates migrate to Cu−Co interfaces for hydrogenation, and adjacent Co domains promote subsequent NH 3 formation. In situ characterizations reveal pronounced Cu–Co synergy, where Co sites regulate *H‐mediated hydrogenation while the balanced surface coverage of *H and *NO 3 − optimizes NH 3 selectivity and yield. Consequently, the optimized Janus Cu−Co catalyst, Janus–Cu 70 Co 30 /NOMC, achieves a peak NH 3 Faradaic efficiency (FE NH3 ) of 95.5% at −500 mA cm −2 and delivers a FE NH3 of 93.1% with an NH 3 yield rate of 4.2 mg h −1 mg cat −1 at −0.4 V vs RHE in an MEA flow cell under low nitrate concentrations. These findings establish phase separation with electronic coupling, enabled by electrochemical time–charge control, as an effective design principle for efficient multistep NO 3 − RR electrocatalysis.

title: Predicting battery stability from electron-ion transport mismatch
abstract: A battery stability prediction model covering LIBs, SIBs, and ZIBs has been proposed. The electron-ion transport mismatch is identified as a key determinant of battery stability. A linear correlation between the battery stability and the electron-ion transport mismatch has been revealed: the closer the transport rates of electrons and ions, the more stable the battery. The battery stability could be predicted rapidly from the electron-ion mismatch, with no need for time-consuming long-term cycling.
